clinician.trajectory_summary: A seven-year-old male with known proximal tubular dysfunction (homozygous SLC4A4 mutation) underwent superficial keratectomy as a day case procedure. He experienced post-operative vomiting but was discharged home stable. Within hours of discharge, he developed acute onset severe left-sided headache with photophobia and phonophobia, accompanied by right-sided hemiparesis (upper and lower limbs), facial asymmetry (change in smile), slurred speech, high fever unresponsive to antipyretics, irritability, and altered mental status (unable to recognize his mother). Neuroimaging (CT brain) was unremarkable, ruling out acute ischemic stroke or hemorrhage. Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable, ruling out CNS infection (meningitis or encephalitis). Laboratory studies on admission revealed electrolyte abnormalities (hypernatremia Na 150 mEq, hypokalemia K 3.1 mEq, low bicarbonate 17), elevated urea (90 mg/dl), normal CRP (0.3 mg/dl), and mild leukocytosis (WBC 11.4×10⁹/L). The patient was admitted to the general pediatric department with the clinical impression of hemiplegic migraine, potentially triggered by emotional stress during anesthesia or exposure to vasoconstrictive medications during the perioperative period. He responded well to supportive care and pain management, and was discharged home with safety netting.
